idiom_name: Jakarta Persistence @Version via Hibernate on the JVM (Spring Data repositories)
implementation_notes: On the JVM the token is provider-managed exactly as in Java: annotate one property of the entity (@Version val version: Int = 0) and let Hibernate read it, add the version predicate to the flush and throw jakarta.persistence.OptimisticLockException when the row moved on; Spring's exception translation surfaces that as org.springframework.dao.OptimisticLockingFailureException at the @Transactional boundary, which is where the retry must start. Kotlin needs the kotlin-jpa compiler plugin so the no-arg constructor JPA requires exists for non-default-constructed entities, and its data classes need care: copy(...) produces a new snapshot that still carries the old token, so either keep the entity a mutable class or treat the copy as a fresh value with an explicitly refreshed version. Nothing in kotlin-stdlib replaces the mechanism; manual forms (R2DBC update row counts, AtomicReference.compareAndSet for in-memory state) remain the fallback outside JPA.
pitfalls: Data-class copy()/equals()/hashCode() include the version property, so copies used as detached snapshots silently smuggle the stale token into later writes.
Without the kotlin-jpa (no-arg) plugin, Hibernate cannot instantiate a class whose properties are all constructor parameters, and lazy loading fails with an InstantiatorException.
Declaring the version as val fights the provider, which must write the field; keep it mutably owned by the provider or restructure so the generated value is not user-visible.
